description: Anyone with AI and machine learning skills are welcome.
summary:
What we developed. SPHEREx Sky Blink is a public web tool where anyone enters a sky position (RA/Dec, sexagesimal text or a target name) and watches SPHEREx images of that patch play like a short video. A FastAPI backend cuts out the patch from FITS data using its WCS, adjusts brightness and serves PNG frames. A plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript page provides the player, slider, five one-click presets and a shareable URL.

How it addresses the challenge. The tool makes moving or changing objects easy to spot through animation, blink compare, difference imaging and stacking. Proper-motion-aware centering keeps fast movers like WISE 0855 in view. A wavelength colour strip and an “Is it real?” badge make the 102 bands understandable and warn when a jump comes from a detector or colour change. Coordinates live in the URL, an embed mode (?embed=1) supports other sites, and a one-line config change switches data releases.

Why it is important. SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months, creating far more data than any person can inspect. Turning that archive into an intuitive animation opens it to students, amateurs and scientists, helping them find asteroids, comets, nearby stars and brown dwarfs. The full pipeline works on realistic mock data, and connecting live IRSA data is the next phase.
details:
1. What does our project do and how does it work?

The system has four layers: Web page → API → Processing → Data. Each layer talks only to the next, so one can be changed without breaking the others.

  1. The user types coordinates, searches by name or clicks a preset.
  2. The page calls /api/frames. The server validates the input (for example, it rejects Dec = 200) and finds images covering that spot.
  3. Processing crops a cutout, applies a brightness stretch (linear, sqrt, log or asinh), optionally matches backgrounds, and applies Normal, Difference or Stack mode.
  4. PNGs are rendered north-up and sent to the page, which preloads and plays them. An info panel shows date, detector and wavelength.
  5. Mock and real data share one frame format, and a config switch selects between them.

2. What benefit does it have?

  • No installation, and no knowledge of FITS, WCS or archive queries is needed.
  • Motion hidden in tables of numbers becomes visible in seconds.
  • Caching, input validation and friendly errors keep it fast and safe to host publicly.
  • Shareable and embeddable links suit classrooms, outreach pages and collaboration.

3. What is the intended impact?

  • Make SPHEREx data accessible to the public and widen participation in discovery.
  • Help researchers screen candidate movers quickly before deeper analysis.
  • Support education through a beginner tutorial, a guided WISE 0855 mission and a practice game.
  • Absorb future data releases with minimal change.

4. Tools used

  • Area - Tools
  • Backend - Python 3.13, FastAPI, uvicorn, astropy, numpy, Pillow, astroquery, pyvo
  • Data Sources - NASA IRSA (SIA/TAP), SIMBAD, Gaia, AllWISE
  • Frontend - Plain HTML, CSS, JavaScript, SVG overlays (no framework)
  • Workflow - Git, Windows virtual environment, plain-Python test runner

5. How is our project creative?

  • Proper-motion-aware centering keeps fast movers in the picture.
  • Expected-path overlay compares where a star should be with where it appears.
  • Blink compare uses the classic technique from the discovery of Pluto.
  • “Is it real?” badge flags false motion from detector or wavelength changes.
  • Wavelength colour strip shows each frame’s band at a glance.
  • Extras: a 3-band colour picture, mover-versus-star spectrum comparison, automatic mover finding, a practice game with hidden fake movers, and GIF and CSV export
